sections.html:
• Type: Stem
  • Origin: Cosmopolitan
  • Height: 20-30+ cm after two months in the tank
  • Light demand: Low
  • CO2: Low

• Common name: Anacharis; other names: Brazilian waterweed, Anacharis densa, Elodea densa, Leafy Elodea, Elodea, Egeria
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (40 litres)
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: any, or floating
  • Growth rate: very fast
  • Placement: background
  • Size (untrimmed): up to 1 m or more
  • Fertilizers: not needed
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: cuttings
  • Colour: green

Egeria densa has long been popular in the aquarium hobby but behaves invasively in many states. It clogs waterways and hydroelectric turbines, out-competes native vegetation and negatively affects the sediment seed bank. Make sure it is not banned where you live and do not buy or sell it illegally.

Anacharis is readily available in most local fish stores and is quite affordable. When shopping, look for sturdy green stems. The leaves should be light to bright green and free from damage and decay. Specimens should be about 15–20 cm long with healthy-looking stems and leaves. Do not buy plants with algae patches or black tints on the foliage.

Although some vendors have stopped selling Anacharis as an aquarium plant because of its invasiveness, it can still be purchased over the Internet.

Quarantine Anacharis before putting it into the aquarium. The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.). It may also have been treated with chemicals (pesticides) to remove parasites, snails and so on, and these chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Anacharis (Egeria densa) is native to South America, in countries such as Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay.

The plant has become naturalized in most parts of the United States and is also present elsewhere in the world, in Africa, Asia and Europe, due to its distribution as an aquarium plant. It is currently naturalized in at least 27 countries in subtropical and temperate regions.

The plant inhabits still and slow-moving waters: lakes, ponds, ditches, streams, rivers and canals, where it forms dense mats and outcompetes native and non-native species.

Anacharis is a perennial aquatic plant. Its foliage varies from light green to bright green, with a lush appearance. The variable pigmentation is probably due to the water conditions where it lives. Its height depends on the depth of the surrounding water: in the wild it can reach up to 3 m, but much less in captivity. A rooting depth of 7 m has been observed in a high-altitude lake in Colombia.

The leaves are finely serrated, narrowly lanceolate and sessile, arranged in whorls of 4–6 (often four per node), 1–3 cm long and 2–5 mm wide, with a pointed tip. The long, delicate green stems are sparsely branched with short internodes, with stringy white roots forming at the base of the plant and at some nodes.

The plant grows to the water surface, then branches spread out horizontally to form a mat or thick canopy. It is dioecious, meaning male and female flowers exist on separate plants. The flowers are about 20 mm across, with 3 broad white petals and 9 yellow anthers. They bloom above the water surface and are rarely seen in the aquarium.

The plant is often confused with Elodea and Hydrilla. Egeria has whorls of 4–6 leaves, Elodea 3 and Hydrilla 5. Egeria densa also has larger leaves, prominent flowers and a smooth midrib on the underside of the leaf.

Taxonomy: Egeria is a genus of three aquatic species in the flowering plant family Hydrocharitaceae, formerly included in Elodea. Egeria densa was described by the French botanist Jules Émile Planchon in 1848. Its earliest report outside its native range is from 1893, when a plant was collected on Long Island, New York.
This plant cannot be kept in nano tanks; it is great for ponds. A minimum tank size of 10 gallons (40 litres) is required. The bigger the better.

Stems grow fast to 40-100 cm and become 2-4 cm wide. Egeria helps prevent algae because it absorbs a great number of nutrients from the water. The growth rate depends largely on the amount of light and nutrition available. Growth does not stop in unfavourable conditions, but the plant turns light in colour and the tendrils grow thin.

The plant is supplied as a bundle of stems or young plants gathered in an anchor. Remove the anchor and split into separate plants. Remove the leaves from the lowest 5 cm (2") of the stems and any damaged leaves. Plant the individual plants with some distance between them into the bottom substrate. Roots will develop soon and the plant starts growing.

Anacharis is easy to care for. Most of the care involves pruning the shoots so they do not overrun the tank when they reach the water surface. Trim regularly for a dense, forest-like look; trimmed plants shoot buds to the sides and become bushy. If the plant is in the background, let it grow densely and clip it only a little.

Under optimal conditions it grows very fast and can double or triple in size in one month. Regular fertilizer helps it grow more vigorously and develop new shoots, although it can thrive without. Carry out partial water changes weekly or every other week, test the water parameters weekly and clean the filter media.

Planting

  1. Gently remove the band holding the stems together.
  2. Examine the stems and remove damaged or dead leaves with a curved blade. The banded area can be cut off if damaged.
  3. Split the stems into separate portions and disinfect them to remove hitchhikers such as tiny snails and micro worms.
  4. Trim the leaves at the base of the stems, as they decay if buried in the substrate.
  5. Bury individual stems about 2.5–5 cm deep so they do not float up shortly after planting. Tweezers help to place them gently.

Avoid planting stems too close to one another, as this promotes unhealthy competition for nutrients. Alternatively, let a few split stems float freely on the surface; use only a few to avoid overcrowding that blocks light.

Floating: if the plant starts rotting after being planted, let it float until it roots itself. Use a weight or wedge it between rocks, driftwood or decor, so no part rots and the roots grow down into the substrate naturally.

Propagation: simply break off portions from mature plants. Take cuttings from long healthy stems; when long aerial roots appear, cut right under the roots and plant into the substrate. Cuttings should ideally be at least 10 cm long, and can be split into smaller pieces. The cuttings develop roots and keep growing; under intense light and with nutrients available, new plants grow rapidly and branch at the nodes.

Temperature: the optimum temperature for Egeria densa in culture is 21 °C. The plant easily tolerates temperatures as low as 15 °C and as high as 28 °C. It also has some tolerance for cold water and can survive winter in a ditch under a cap of ice, although freezing is lethal.

pH: 6.0–8.0.

Hardness: Anacharis generally does not care about hardness and does well at 2–20 GH. It can tolerate hard water. Moving it from very soft to hard water can be tricky and the plant can melt, but moving it from hard to soft water does not cause this problem.

Salinity: in laboratory conditions Egeria densa tolerates up to 8 g/l, and in its habitat in the Valdivia River basin 5 g/l. A salinity of around 1 g/l promotes growth and biomass production. At 2 g/l and higher its development gradually deteriorates, with reduced growth, fewer roots and a sharp drop in photosynthesis.

Light: the plant needs moderate to high lighting to photosynthesize and grow optimally. Under intense light it releases a great deal of oxygen. Ideally keep the lights on at least 8 hours daily. Its photosynthetic rate increases in a nearly linear fashion with increasing light. At low light levels, growth favours elongation of shoots (instead of more shoots) and development of upper (canopy) branches.

Substrate: Anacharis can grow either planted or floating, because it can extract nutrients from both the sediment and the water column. Once planted it starts growing much faster. It grows in almost any substrate; a good choice is aquarium gravel or sand, preferably with aqua soil underneath to provide nutrients.

CO2 and fertilizers: the plant thrives in tanks without CO2 and does not rely heavily on fertilizers. For optimal growth and a lush appearance, add fertilizer from time to time (weekly or bi-weekly).

Important: with shrimp in the tank, high CO2 and high copper levels are extremely dangerous to them, and most fertilizers contain copper.

Anacharis can be paired with many aquatic species, though it suits community tanks with small peaceful fish that will not rip its delicate shoots apart.

Compatible fish: Corydoras catfish, neon tetras, zebra danio, ember tetras, guppies, Endlers, mollies, Otocinclus catfish, pygmy cory catfish.

Compatible shrimp: cherry shrimp, snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, ghost shrimp, Amano shrimp, blue tiger shrimp, blue velvet shrimp, vampire shrimp, bamboo shrimp, cardinal shrimp, red nose shrimp, etc.

Compatible snails: Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.

Avoid species that may find Anacharis palatable, e.g. koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches and African cichlids. Most crayfish and freshwater crabs are also a bad combination, as they cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank; unless the plant is left floating, it is a no go.
The cosmopolitan Egeria densa is a good plant for beginners, and its rapid growth helps create a balance in the aquarium from the start.

Problems

Melting: plants may wither days after planting, due to a change in environment or a problem with planting. Introducing Anacharis to a new tank with different water chemistry stresses it and it sheds old leaves. Give it time to acclimate. Even after acclimation, harsh swings in water chemistry can still cause leaf shedding and decay at the bottom. Letting the plant float for a while helps: it survives and grows roots, which can then be rooted into the substrate without weighing it down.

Dormant state: sometimes the plant just sits in the tank, neither growing nor dying. Check the light: start with a photoperiod of 10 hours daily, then if that does not help slowly increase light intensity. If it is not planted, plant it. Add nutrients and trim it. If Anacharis takes over all the available space, it almost stops growing even if light, feeding and temperature remain the same.

Overgrowth: it may overrun the tank if left unattended and shade the plants at the bottom. Trim and discard it from time to time to prevent overcrowding and shadowing at the surface.

Discoloration: it needs bright light to photosynthesize and keep vibrant colour. In low light it may look pale green or slightly yellowish. Keep water quality good with weekly partial water changes and ideal water values.

Benefits

Aquascape: its shape and form give a beautiful contrast and make an excellent decorative addition to a jungle aquascape.

Removal of excess nutrients: Egeria densa has heavy metal absorption properties and helps absorb harmful substances from fish waste, decayed plant matter and tap water, such as nitrate, CO2, ammonia and phosphate. It shows a clear preference for ammonium over nitrate, and phosphorus may be more limiting for it than nitrogen. It does remove nitrate, but must convert it back to ammonium, which takes a lot of energy, and it competes with beneficial bacteria for ammonium.

Algae control: it outcompetes algae for nutrients and suppresses their growth. It has allelopathic qualities, excreting substances that inhibit the growth of blue-green algae and phytoplankton.

Hiding place: it serves as cover and shade for inverts, small fish, fry and shrimp.

Foraging place: it acts as a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.

Oxygenation: it oxygenates and aerates the tank water.
